sample.summary: Following the end of discussions regarding Mr. Collins's proposal, Mrs. Bennet remains ill-humored and Mr. Collins treats Elizabeth with stiffness and resentful silence, shifting his attentions to Miss Lucas while maintaining his plan to stay until Saturday. The next morning, the Bennet sisters walk to Meryton to inquire about Mr. Wickham. Wickham meets them and privately admits to Elizabeth that he stayed away from the Netherfield ball to avoid an unpleasant encounter with Mr. Darcy. Elizabeth approves of his restraint. Wickham and another officer then walk back with the sisters to Longbourn, where Wickham is introduced to Mr. and Mrs. Bennet. Shortly after their return, Jane receives a letter from Caroline Bingley. Once the officers leave, Jane takes Elizabeth upstairs to read it. Caroline writes that the Netherfield party has gone to London to follow Mr. Bingley and will not return this winter, adding that Mr. Bingley admires Georgiana Darcy and expressing hope that they will marry. Jane interprets this as proof of Bingley's indifference and believes he will not come back. Elizabeth disputes this, asserting that Caroline knows Bingley loves Jane and wants to keep them apart to promote a match with Miss Darcy. Although Jane refuses to think Caroline is intentionally deceptive, Elizabeth gradually persuades her to remain hopeful of Bingley's return. The sisters agree to tell Mrs. Bennet only of the party's departure. Though initially upset, Mrs. Bennet soon consoles herself by anticipating Bingley's return for dinner and planning to serve two full courses.
sample.synopsis: Wickham visits Longbourn; Caroline Bingley writes that Bingley left for London and favors Miss Darcy, prompting Elizabeth to persuade a disheartened Jane to remain hopeful.

sample.summary: As the regiment enters its final week in Meryton, Mrs. Bennet, Kitty, and Lydia lament the upcoming departure and wish to visit Brighton. Lydia soon receives an invitation from Mrs. Forster, the colonel's young wife, to accompany her there. Lydia and Mrs. Bennet celebrate, while Kitty complains about being left behind. Privately, Elizabeth asks Mr. Bennet to forbid the trip, warning that Lydia's unrestrained behavior will fix her character as a determined flirt, mislead Kitty, and damage the family's reputation. Mr. Bennet refuses, reasoning that Longbourn would have no peace if Lydia stayed, Colonel Forster will keep her from serious mischief, and Brighton will teach her her own insignificance. Elizabeth leaves disappointed, while Lydia and Mrs. Bennet remain ignorant of her intervention. On the regiment's final day, several officers dine at Longbourn. Displeased by Mr. Wickham's recent efforts to renew his attentions toward her, Elizabeth answers his questions about Hunsford by noting that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy spent three weeks at Rosings. She adds that Darcy improves on acquaintance, clarifying that knowing him better allows his disposition to be better understood. Wickham looks alarmed and agitated, then suggests Darcy only behaves cautiously to please his aunt and secure a match with Miss de Bourgh. Elizabeth smiles slightly without pursuing the topic, and they part civilly. Afterward, Lydia leaves with Mrs. Forster to depart for Brighton the next morning, amid Mrs. Bennet's enthusiastic wishes and Kitty's envious tears.
sample.synopsis: Mr. Bennet rejects Elizabeth's plea to stop Lydia's Brighton trip. At a farewell dinner, Elizabeth unsettles Wickham by praising Darcy before Lydia departs with Mrs. Forster.

sample.summary: Narrative momentum compresses tightly around the primary courtship and elopement arcs, leaving a handful of secondary threads—such as Colonel Fitzwilliam's prospects, Anne de Bourgh's future, and the Collinses' retreat—to drop off once their immediate plot pressure ends.

firstFinding.headline: Colonel Fitzwilliam's financial dilemma and role as witness disappear after Kent
bullets: Chapters 31-33 invest significant page time in establishing Fitzwilliam as a charming foil to Darcy, caught between attraction to Elizabeth and his need as a younger son to marry for money.

Darcy explicitly names him as the corroborating witness for his letter's claims, yet Elizabeth never consults him, and he departs Rosings in Chapter 37 without ever reappearing—even as Georgiana's co-guardian at Pemberley or at the weddings in Chapter 61.
firstFinding.recommendedAction: Add a brief line in Chapter 61 or Chapter 60 updating Colonel Fitzwilliam's marital or guardianship status and confirming his reaction to Darcy's match.
firstFinding.subject: Colonel Fitzwilliam subplot

supportingRefs.quote: For the truth of everything here related, I can appeal more particularly to the testimony of Colonel Fitzwilliam, who, from our near relationship and constant intimacy, and still more as one of the executors of my father’s will, has been unavoidably acquainted with every particular of these transactions.

The two gentlemen left Rosings the next morning; and Mr. Collins having been in waiting near the lodges, to make them his parting obeisance, was able to bring home the pleasing intelligence of their appearing in very good health, and in as tolerable spirits as could be expected, after the melancholy scene so lately gone through at Rosings.
